paragraphs: For two distinct odd primes, construct both oriented Gauss half-system counts at once. The preceding finite-fold, bounded-remainder, permutation, and Euler/Gauss lemmas show that each count classifies the corresponding cross-residue proposition.

Eisenstein's lattice count supplies the shared parity relation: after transporting both counts modulo two, their sum is the product of the two half-prime parameters. The theorem retains all witnesses, so the two final reciprocity cases can reuse one provenance-preserving data package.
distinct_odd_primes_gauss_eisenstein_dat.title: Build the common Gauss–Eisenstein data package

paragraphs: Write the two odd primes as successors of twice their half-prime parameters. Construct the common Gauss–Eisenstein data package once and unpack its two residue classifications, two parity transports, and the lattice-count identity.

For the same-status implication, feed the hypothesis that one half-prime parameter is even into the constructive same-parity endpoint. For the opposite-status implication, feed the hypothesis that both half-prime parameters are odd into the opposite-parity endpoint. Pair the two implications under the original quantifiers.
quadratic_reciprocity_combined.title: Combine the two sign-free reciprocity cases

paragraphs: Construct and unpack the shared oriented Gauss–Eisenstein counts. When both half-prime parameters are odd, their product is odd, so the Eisenstein identity forces the two Gauss counts to have opposite parity.

The two count classifications then say that exactly one of the cross-residue propositions holds. This is the three-mod-four case of quadratic reciprocity, expressed without a sign or Legendre-symbol primitive.
conditional_qres_opposite_status_from_or.title: Derive opposite residue status in the three-mod-four case

paragraphs: Construct and unpack the shared oriented Gauss–Eisenstein counts. If one half-prime parameter is even, their product is even; the Eisenstein identity and the two modulo-two transports therefore force the Gauss counts to have the same parity.
Each count's parity is already equivalent to the truth status of its cross-residue proposition, so the two propositions are equivalent. This is the one-mod-four case of quadratic reciprocity.
conditional_qres_same_status_from_orient.title: Derive equal residue status when one prime is one modulo four
